title: Seneca's last hours
hook: ordered to die by Nero, he tells his friends he leaves them the one thing he has, the image of his life

segments.voice: Yesterday: consolatio, the letter Seneca sent from exile to comfort his mother. Comfort the comforter.

A soldier arrives at a country house with the emperor's order: the man inside is to die. The man is Seneca. He came home from exile to tutor a boy named Nero; the boy became emperor, and for a few years Seneca helped steer the empire. Then Nero changed. Seneca tried to step away, even offering to hand back his fortune. Then a plot to kill Nero was uncovered. Whether Seneca was part of it, nobody knows. Nero didn't need to know.
screen: `A SOLDIER AT THE DOOR.` → `THE TUTOR AND THE EMPEROR.` → `A PLOT AGAINST NERO.`

segments.voice: The Roman historian Tacitus, writing some decades later, tells it plainly. Seneca, calm, asks for his will so he can leave gifts to his friends. The soldier refuses. So he turns to the friends around his table. Since he can't thank them as they deserve, he'll leave them the only thing he still has, and the most beautiful: the image of his life. Remember it, and they'll be known for good character and faithful friendship. His friends start weeping. Seneca, gently and then more firmly, asks where their philosophy has gone, all those years of preparing for exactly this. His wife, Paulina, is with him and wants to die with him. Tacitus says Nero, not wanting to seem too cruel, ordered her kept alive; she lived on some years, pale for the rest of her life, remembering him. Seneca died, as ordered. This isn't told to make death look noble. It's told for one line. The money, the house, the will: all of it could be taken. What was left was the image of how he'd lived. Not a statue, not even his writings: the picture of a life his friends would carry. And a question for any of us, long before the end. If the people who love you described the image of your life in one line, what would it be? Is it the line you'd choose?
screen: `THE SOLDIER REFUSES THE WILL.` · `THE ONLY THING HE STILL HAS.` · `WHERE HAS YOUR PHILOSOPHY GONE?` · `PAULINA LIVES ON.` · then, large: `THE IMAGE OF A LIFE.`

segments.voice: This one is about living. Sit, let the breath settle, and picture the people who love you around a table, remembering how you were, not what you achieved: kind, funny, always showed up. Let a phrase come, then ask whether it's the image you'd choose, and what you'd add.
imago vitae, Latin for the image of a life, which is what Seneca left his friends when he was ordered to die.
Your line: the image of a life. Yours is still being made, one ordinary day at a time. That's day thirty-three.

original.note: Latin: the image of a life. Tacitus reports Seneca leaving his friends imaginem vitae suae, the image of his life.

notes: SENSITIVE: an ordered death. Written with no method detail (Tacitus describes the manner at length; omitted). Framed as not making death noble; the practice says explicitly it's about living.
Annals 15.62: refused tablets for his will, he leaves friends 'the one thing, and yet the noblest, that he had: the image of his life' (paraphrased; Church & Brodribb not on the list). Confirm.
Paulina: Nero ordered her death prevented (15.64); she lived 'a few years' with a pallor. Confirm.
The 'good years' of Nero's early reign (quinquennium Neronis) attributed to Seneca and Burrus's influence; stated loosely.
Tacitus wrote c. 110–120 CE ('about fifty years later'). Confirm.
Imago as ancestor mask: standard; confirm the trapdoor note.
